poiHYD-desc:
India, along with Pakistan, was one of the instigators of the Great Mistake. The nuclear conflict between them turned the unresolved problems of the old world into the catastrophe that followed, and as its epicenter, the subcontinent was the region most affected by it. Most of the north is a society trying to find its feet again. Most of the south is impoverished and divided between warlords. Pakistan and Bangladesh are filled with destitution beyond human comprehension.

The Pact of Hyderabad is the loose bloc that has grown out of those ruins. Its members include Bharat, Kavitha, Rajasthan, Odisha, Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka, Tamilakam, West Bengal and East Bengal, together with Punjab, Sindh, Kashmir, Balochistan and Pashtunistan to the north-west. It is closer to an extensive non-aggression pact than to a union. Its members trade, tolerate one another and keep their armies at home, and for now that is enough.

Bharat is the centre of the Pact. It sits at the crossroads of the great highways and holds the industrial heartland of the North, and its leader, Raj Thakur, is the one figure whom most of the bloc's rulers will listen to. From coal to iron, many resources flow through its markets, and its relations with the Pan-Asian Cooperative remain cold and wary.

The Pact stands at a crossroads. The prophet who holds it together is dying, and his life may be the only thing preventing the subcontinent from collapsing into a battle royale. But even if he dies, Bharat can make sure that he lives on.

The old India has finished licking its wounds.
HYDpoi001-desc:
Known to his followers as the modern Gandhi, and to some as the modern Vivekananda, Raj Thakur is the leader and prophet of the new India. He began his career as president of the Indian successor state, but his political thought soon slipped into popular thought, not as a doctrine but as a way of life. The people yearned for more of his teaching, and over the years it morphed into a syncretic religious doctrine that spread across northern India almost as quickly as the radiation had decades before.

Wisdom and meditation, though pillars of the soul, cannot sustain the weight of time. A revered and mystical figure, Thakur has a loyal following in Bharat, and his spiritual connections and ancient wisdom have made him the voice of guidance for the whole Pact. He has long suffered from recurrent pancreatic cancer, and his mind has persevered despite his deteriorating body. His more devoted followers read the fact that he is still alive as a miracle.

Now, however, his illness has surpassed even what 22nd century science can cure, and his condition is terminal. He accepted his death long ago, though perhaps the same cannot be said for his followers. Despite decades of peace and meditation, the great fracture in his serene mind is his dread of what might become of India after he is gone.
HYDpoi002-desc:
Bharat sits at the crossroads of most major Indian highways and lays claim to the industrial heartland of the North. Despite decades of setbacks and political scandals, its central government carries the most legitimate claim to the Indian Republic of old.

Led by the aged politician and spiritual leader Raj Thakur, Bharat has barely managed to sustain a loose alliance of the warlords who have long been fighting over the old India. The alliance is more akin to an extensive non-aggression pact, but this temporary unity has given Bharat an enviable position as the crossroads of inter-warlord trade. Thakur's extensive compound has also become home to influential individuals from all over the country and beyond, attracting foreign talent and much needed muscle.
HYDpoi003-desc:
Although Raj Thakur carries an extraordinary amount of influence within Bharat, and the loyalty of his people has never been in question, military interests have always been a pressing matter. In his early days, when Bharat was still an unstable warzone between army elements, raiders and tides of refugees, the young and inexperienced leader chose to ally himself with the 4th Republican Army of India. The alliance helped him cement power and ward off opportunistic invaders, but it also allowed a rot of spirit to set in.

It was not until 2137 that the kettle boiled over. Military elements led by one Krishna Aurora tried to march on the capital and force Thakur into the position of a puppet. The visionary was saved only by the timely arrival of his elite guards, who arrested Aurora and convinced the army to stand down. The following years were spent detoothing most of the military and making the high command completely subordinate to Thakur's civilian administration.

The only autonomous part of the army now is the Officers' Club, where ambitious generals and aging commanders plot to usher in a return of their once powerful force.
